the AAMI subjects are genetically distinct from the controls, but the APOE polymorphism alone is not a sufficient explanation of the AAMI phenotype.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the APOC4 polymorphism, which is located within the APOE gene and is in strong linkage disequilibrium with APOE, may be the most important genetic factor for the development of AAMI, but the APOC5 and APOC6 polymorphisms may also play some role.
the genetic polymorphisms of APOE and, to a lesser extent, APOC1 may contribute to the development of age-associated memory impairment.

The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic factors may contribute to the etiology of memory impairment in the elderly, and that the APOE gene is not the only one to be considered in the study of cognitive aging.
AAMI subjects have a different genetic background compared with normally aging subjects in the APOE and the APOC loci.
